Histomaps.org

Welcome to the Histomap

History is usually read one story at a time. The Histomap lets you see many of those stories at once: civilizations flowing through time, with people and events placed inside the larger sweep of history.

Scroll through the centuries, zoom into crowded periods, and select ribbons, lifelines and events to explore their context. The map is designed to reward both a quick glance and deep wandering.

The width of a civilization stream follows John B. Sparks’s original visual language of relative historical power and influence. It is an interpretive historical view, not a precise quantitative measure.

Where this might go: Histomaps.org can grow into richer historical maps, new ways to explore lives and events, and eventually experimental Histomaps of the possible futures that extend from the present.

This introduction appears on your first visit.

About this implementation

A visual argument about history

The Histomap began with John B. Sparks’s 1931 chart, which compressed thousands of years of history into a single field of colored streams. Histomaps.org is an independent interactive implementation by J. Hunter Sizemore, built from that visual idea and extended with interactive streams, events, lifelines and historical context.

How to read the map

Stream width follows Sparks’s basic language of relative historical power and influence. It should be read as an interpretive visual judgment, not as a measured quantity of population, territory, wealth or moral importance.

What is original here

The interactive interface, software implementation, map behavior, event and lifeline systems, data organization, editorial structure, original writing and substantial historical curation in this edition are part of the Histomaps.org implementation. The 1931 source is credited throughout to John B. Sparks.

Sources, corrections and uncertainty

This public preview combines reconstruction of the Sparks source with later historical research and explicit corrections. Dates, boundaries, labels and historical interpretations can be uncertain or contested. The project aims to make those distinctions clearer as the map develops rather than disguise judgment as precision.

Public preview: the map is being prepared for wider release and will continue to change in response to historical review, usability testing and reader feedback.

1886–1949 · England → United States

The creator of the Histomap

John Bertram Sparks

Engineer · business executive · historical chartmaker

Biography

John Bertram Sparks was born in St Ives, Huntingdon, England, in 1886. He studied electrical engineering at Finsbury Technical College from 1902 to 1904 and worked on early power and electrification projects in Baghdad, Norway, Sweden and London. He later emigrated to the United States and pursued a business career; by the end of his life he was a director of Nestlé’s Milk Products Inc. in New York.

History and visual explanation were a serious avocation. In 1931 Sparks created The Histomap: Four Thousand Years of World History, published by Histomap, Inc. in Chicago and printed and distributed by Rand McNally. Its five-foot vertical field turned states, nations and empires into colored streams whose changing widths represented Sparks’s judgment of their relative power. He later developed companion Histomaps of evolution and religion. Sparks died on 22 December 1949; his daughter Anne Sparks Glanz continued updating and publishing the charts.

Perspective to keep in mind

Sparks’s charts are visual arguments, not neutral measurements. His Histomap of Religion explicitly says that, where numerical criteria were unavailable, “relative contemporary significance” was judged from a liberal Christian viewpoint. His history and evolution charts also use Western power hierarchies and period racial/national categories that modern scholarship does not accept. Histomaps.org treats those assumptions as part of the historical artifact to examine, rather than a worldview to inherit.
